    AI Overview
    Immunization is
    a safe, highly effective process that makes individuals resistant to infectious diseases by stimulating the immune system with vaccines to produce antibodies. It prevents serious illness, hospitalization, and death, protecting both individuals and communities. Routine vaccines, such as Tdap, flu, and MMR, are essential across all ages, with common minor side effects including fever or soreness. 
    How Immunization Works
    Vaccines stimulate the body’s immune system to create an "imitation" infection, which is a mild form of the actual disease, without causing the disease itself. This process teaches the immune system to recognize and fight the pathogen, enabling it to combat the real disease upon future exposure. 
    • Immune Response: The body develops T lymphocytes and B lymphocytes that "remember" how to fight the infection.
    • Protection: Once vaccinated, the body is primed to fight, often preventing disease entirely or significantly shortening its duration. 
    Key Benefits of Immunization 
    • Disease Prevention: Protects against, or reduces the severity of, diseases like influenza, tetanus, measles, polio, and COVID-19.
    • Public Health Impact: Prevents thousands of deaths and millions of illness cases, serving as a key health achievement.
    • Individual & Community Protection: Protects not only the vaccinated person but also those around them who cannot be vaccinated. 
    Types of Immunization & Common Vaccines
    Immunizations include routine pediatric and adult vaccines to create immunity. 
    • Childhood Immunizations: DTaP (diphtheria, tetanus, pertussis), Hib, polio, MMR (measles, mumps, rubella), and chickenpox.
    • Adult Vaccines: Annual flu shot, Tdap, shingles, and RSV. 
    Side Effects of Immunization
    Immunizations are safe, but can cause minor side effects as the body builds immunity, including: 
    • Fever.
    • Soreness or swelling at the injection site. 
    Vaccine Schedule & Access
    Routine vaccines are crucial to prevent outbreaks. Parents should start vaccine conversations early, with schedules designed to protect against infections from infancy through adulthood. Pharmacies like Walgreens and medical offices offer these vaccines, with options for appointments or walk-ins.

    Purpose. What is the purpose of immunization?
    About this result
    Feedback
    An AI Overview is not available for this searchCan't generate an AI overview right now. Try again later.
    AI Overview
    The primary purpose of immunization is to safely build lasting immunity against infectious diseases, protecting individuals from serious illness, complications, or death. By inducing an immune response without causing the disease itself, vaccines prepare the body to recognize and fight pathogens, while also creating community immunity that prevents disease spread. 
    Key purposes and benefits include:
    • Preventing Deadly Diseases:
      Vaccines protect against dangerous pathogens like measles, polio, diphtheria, and COVID-19. 
    • Building Lasting Protection:
      Vaccines enable the body to produce antibodies and memory cells, which recognize and combat specific viruses or bacteria in the future. 
    • Community Immunity (Herd Immunity):
      Widespread vaccination reduces the spread of diseases, protecting vulnerable individuals who cannot be vaccinated, such as infants or those with weakened immune systems. 
    • Reducing Mortality and Morbidity:
      Immunization has drastically reduced global mortality, turning deadly diseases into preventable ones. 
    • Cost-Effective Healthcare:
      Vaccination is a safe, effective, and economical way to prevent disease rather than treating it.

      Side Effects. What are the side effects of immunization?
      About this result
      Feedback
      An AI Overview is not available for this searchCan't generate an AI overview right now. Try again later.
      AI Overview
      Common side effects of immunization are generally mild, temporary, and indicate the immune system is building protection. Typical reactions include pain, swelling, or redness at the injection site, low-grade fever, headaches, and fatigue. These usually last 1–3 days and are manageable with care. 
      Common Usage Examples (Symptoms)
      • Local Reactions: Soreness, swelling, tenderness, and redness at the injection site. 
      • Systemic Reactions: Low-grade fever, mild headache, muscle aches, chills, and fatigue. 
      • Children Specific: Increased fussiness or irritability, loss of appetite, and reduced activity, typically starting within 24 hours. 
      • Other Potential Reactions: Mild vomiting, rash, or diarrhea, particularly with certain vaccines. 
      Rare Serious Side Effects (Adverse Events)
      • Anaphylaxis: Severe allergic reaction occurring within minutes to hours, characterized by difficulty breathing or facial swelling. 
      • Fainting: Sometimes occurs after injections, particularly in adolescents. 
      • High Fever: Fevers above
        102∘F102 raised to the composed with power F
        (
        39∘C39 raised to the composed with power C
        )         or persistent reactions.         
      Synonyms for Vaccine Side Effects Adverse events following immunization (AEFI), Vaccine reactions, Local reactions, Systemic reactions, and Immunization reactions.
      What to Do & When to Seek Help
      • Management: Use a cool, wet washcloth on the sore area to reduce discomfort. 
      • When to Call a Doctor: If the reaction is severe, unexpected, or lasts more than a few days. 
      Commonly Used Vaccine Types and Related Reactions
      • COVID-19 Vaccines: Often cause fatigue, headache, and muscle pain. 
      • MMR/Chickenpox: May cause a fever or rash 1–4 weeks later. 
      • HPV Vaccine: High incidence of injection site soreness.

        Feedback
        We now have vaccines to prevent more than 30 life-threatening diseases and infections, helping people of all ages live longer, healthier lives. Immunization currently prevents 3.5 million to 5 million deaths every year from diseases like diphtheria, tetanus, pertussis (whooping cough), influenza and measles.
